verdict_reason: The sheet holds 30 tiles from only 2 photographers (18 from one account with consecutive ids, 12 from another), i.e. two trip albums, and the subjects are scattered right across Hanoi: eleven frames inside the Temple of Literature (Khue Van Cac, the doctors' stelae on stone turtles, the Thien Quang well and its stele galleries, the bell pavilion, bronze censers), the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum with 'HO-CHI-MINH' carved on it, the One Pillar Pagoda, the Ho Chi Minh Museum's cloud relief, the Ly Thai To statue, Hoan Kiem Lake with the Turtle Tower, the Ngoc Son temple gate with its giant Phuc and Loc characters, four frames in the Vietnam Military History Museum aircraft yard, and a run of Old Quarter street scenes with a 'LE HOI TRUNG THU PHO CO 2007' banner. The Temple of Literature alone is about 1.8 km from this pin and the Mausoleum about 2 km; no single coordinate can hold this set. Classic whole-album-pinned-to-one-point behaviour.

photos.evidence: Looking down from an upper floor over sweeping brown pantile roofs with white cement dragon ridge scrolls onto a courtyard holding an open timber bell pavilion with a large bronze bell hung between posts, stone lanterns and bonsai in white pots, brick paving, and city buildings visible beyond the perimeter wall. The bell pavilion, stone lanterns and roof style match the Thai Hoc rear courtyard of the Temple of Literature, whose Khue Van Cac gate this photographer also shot (12035608954).

A large clipped-hedge display panel with a red flower diamond and green fret border, three outsized cream cylinders with red tips (oversized ceremonial incense sticks or brushes) leaning against an old grey rendered wall with a Vietnamese meander frieze, and a temple tile roof and frangipani behind. Temple grounds under festival dressing; placed with the rest of this photographer's Temple of Literature run, but nothing here names it, hence the lower confidence.

A shrine bay framed by gilded carved dragon-and-cloud panels, red lacquered columns and a red backboard, with a seated bronze figure in court robes and cap on a raised throne, an elaborate red-and-gold altar table in front, two tall blue-and-white porcelain vases flanking it, and offerings and incense. A Confucian-style seated deity shrine consistent with the Temple of Literature's Confucius and Chu Van An altars; no plaque legible, so placed largely by continuity with this photographer's other frames.

An open timber pavilion of heavy dark posts under a double tiled roof with white dragon ridge ornaments, housing a large bronze bell, standing on a paved terrace with white-potted bonsai and stone lanterns; the temple's tiled roofs are at the right and modern buildings with red banners show over the wall behind. Same bell pavilion as 12035206655, from ground level.

A wide brick-paved courtyard with a large bronze tripod censer with dragon handles at its centre flanked by bonsai in stone pots, facing a long low hall with red columns, red-lacquered doors and a broad brown tile roof, visitors moving along its verandah and mature trees behind. The proportions and red colonnade match the Temple of Literature's Dai Thanh / Thai Hoc halls.

A long open timber gallery under a brown pantile roof with a small raised central pavilion, closed off with red rope, standing beside a rectangular pool edged with a white balustrade and beds of purple-flowered hedge, with an enormous banyan behind. That is one of the two stele galleries beside the Thien Quang well in the Temple of Literature's third courtyard.

A brick-paved court between two dark timber halls with open lattice sides, looking towards a tile-roofed gate hall with a red-lacquered board over its opening and white dragon ridge ornaments; frangipani and bonsai in stone troughs line both sides, and a modern block shows over the roofs. Same complex and same paving, bonsai troughs and rope barriers as the other Temple of Literature frames.

A large bronze tripod censer with a domed dragon-crested lid and dragon handles on a lotus-carved bronze base, standing on grey stone paving with a long tile-roofed hall and clipped shrubs behind. The same censer type and paving as 12035487733; placed by continuity.

Inside an open tile-roofed gallery: a large carved stone tortoise with its head raised, its flat back cut to receive a stele, roped off with red rope on a red carpet, with framed wooden explanatory boards on the plastered piers. Stone-tortoise stele bases under an open gallery are the Temple of Literature's doctoral stelae.

The two-storey gate pavilion read directly: a square stone base with a single arched passage, its pylons carved with dragons, carrying an upper timber storey with red balustrades, a round window with radiating spokes, and an ornate tiled roof with dragon finials; through the arch a courtyard with a stone-railed platform and further halls. That is Khue Van Cac, the emblem gate of the Temple of Literature.

A carved white stone trough planter holding a rockery bonsai on brick paving, with a mango-like tree, a red tiled verandah and a souvenir counter with racks of goods behind, and further tile roofs beyond. Consistent with the Temple of Literature's rear courtyards where this photographer's other frames are; no legible sign, so confidence stays moderate.

A tall dark bronze statue of a robed king in a square cap on a stone plinth lettered 'LY THAI TO', on a broad stepped granite platform with beds of red and yellow flowers, clipped topiary and white bollards, motorcyclists passing in the foreground and trees and a pale modern building behind. The plinth inscription names it: the Ly Thai To statue in the garden on Dinh Tien Hoang beside Hoan Kiem Lake.

A monumental interior: a bronze statue of Ho Chi Minh with one hand raised, backed by a large stylised relief of clouds and rock and a gilded disc, set against pale marble cladding with dark red pilasters, with potted plants and visitors carrying flowers at the base. A hall built around a raised-hand Ho Chi Minh statue with a cloud relief matches the Ho Chi Minh Museum's central hall; nothing is lettered, so I hold it at moderate confidence.

A small square timber shrine with an upswept tiled roof and dragon ridge ornaments, carried on a single thick stone pillar rising out of a square pond, its water reflecting the underside; a white balustrade with green-glazed openwork panels runs round the pond and a stone staircase with a rendered parapet climbs at the left. That is Chua Mot Cot, the One Pillar Pagoda.

Grey-green lake water with the small stone Turtle Tower on its islet in mid-lake - three tapering tiers with arched openings - trees along the left bank and a skyline of white and pastel city blocks behind, with a few pedal boats out on the water.

A timber pavilion with a double upswept tiled roof standing above a wide flight of stone steps with rendered parapets, beside water enclosed by the same white balustrade with green-glazed openwork panels as 12041458975, with dense trees around. Same pond balustrade and stair as the One Pillar Pagoda frame, so the adjoining Dien Huu shrine in that compound.

A stone triple gateway on a rockery, its two large panels bearing single huge red Chinese characters - 'Loc' on the left pylon and 'Phuc' on the right - with vertical columns of smaller Chinese inscription beside them, visitors on the steps between and lake water and trees behind. That is the outer gate of Den Ngoc Son on Hoan Kiem Lake.

The grey granite mausoleum read from its own inscription 'HO-CHI-MINH' cut across the entablature, above a colonnade of square piers on a broad stepped podium, with white-uniformed sentries at the red-curtained doorway, two gold state emblems on stands, clipped conifers along the front and the parade ground in front.

A Bell UH-1 lettered 'U.S. AIR FORCE' with serial 17651 and a USAF star-and-bar, on a concrete plinth in a paved yard; to the left the museum's heap of crushed American aircraft wreckage with a missile and armour beside it, at the right a cream colonial building with an arcaded verandah, and uniformed soldiers walking through. Same yard, wreckage pile and colonial block as the Military History Museum frames in the piles at 105.8398,21.0327 and 105.8402,21.0328.

A street market stall hung with a huge mass of foil balloons and red festival toys, in front of ochre French-colonial shophouses with green louvred shutters, motorbikes threading past. A red vertical banner at the left reads 'LE HOI TRUNG THU PHO CO 2007' - the Old Quarter Mid-Autumn Festival - which fixes the district but not the street; the toy and lantern trade for that festival runs along Hang Ma and Luong Van Can.

An elderly woman in a conical hat sitting with her tea things and red plastic stools against a grey plaster wall entirely covered in red hand-sprayed 'KHOAN CAT BE TONG' concrete-drilling adverts with mobile numbers (0912936662, 0902066155, 0906251595 and others). Vietnamese street, but the numbers are advertising, not an address, and no street plate or shopfront is in frame.

A flower seller in a conical hat and checked shirt at her bicycle, its rear rack loaded with red ixora and white lilies, beside a parked motorbike, in front of a yellow louvred shutter and a blue notice board whose Vietnamese text about procedures and regulations is not legible enough to identify the office. No street plate or number.

A polished gold-coloured bust of Ho Chi Minh photographed against a plain scarlet wall with a gold hammer-and-sickle emblem above it. No room, caption, window or architectural detail is visible, so nothing places it - such busts stand in party offices and museums all over Vietnam.

Extreme wide-angle close-up of a rusted, twisted steel band with star shapes cut out of it, casting a shadow on concrete, with barrels and a pale building blurred behind. The same star-pierced rusted steel element stands in front of the crushed-aircraft wreckage pile in this photographer's 1916850020, which places it in the Military History Museum yard; on its own this frame would be unidentifiable.

Wide-angle view of a curling rusted steel sculpture pierced with star cut-outs on a circular concrete pad on grass, with the museum's tall heap of mangled American aircraft wreckage rising directly behind it, a missile nose at the left edge and low white buildings beyond. Same wreckage monument as the other Military History Museum frames.

Fisheye shot from close under the nose of a UH-1 helicopter numbered 651 on its concrete plinth, with a second aircraft and the crushed-wreckage heap behind it, bonsai pots along the paving and a visitor walking past a low colonial building at the right. Same helicopter and yard as 1916054211.

A festival shop overflowing onto the pavement with red silk lanterns, coloured paper lanterns and toys hung on bamboo poles under an ochre colonial shophouse with a balustraded balcony; a white sign at the right reads '...HAU HIEU / CHU XOP / IN TH...', i.e. the slogan-and-foam-lettering trade. That trade plus lanterns is the Hang Ma stock in trade, and the same photographer's 2007 Mid-Autumn banner shot is on the same walk, but no street plate is visible so I stop at district.

A bird-cage maker's shopfront: dozens of bamboo bird cages hung in rows from a rail and stacked behind, under a gold script sign whose readable fragment ends '... Ha ...' (I upscaled it to 5x and the rest stayed illegible), with a tree trunk in front and the shop's household clutter behind. Old Quarter craft-street character, nothing that names the street.

An ochre-washed temple facade flush with the pavement: red-tiled coping, black-lacquered arched double doors, a tall red vertical board with gold Chinese characters (reading in part 'dong tho tam ton ... chinh tong'), a framed 'CONG TRINH' restoration plaque whose smaller lines are illegible even at 8x, and five men drinking tea on plastic stools on the footway with a motorbike parked alongside. A small pagoda or communal house of the sort embedded in Old Quarter streets, but the plaque - the one thing that would name it - cannot be read.

An old bicycle with a metal case beside it leaning against a peeling ochre wall stencilled with red 'KHOAN CAT BE TONG' drilling adverts and phone numbers (0902066155, 0906219986 and others) - the same wall and the same advert numbers as 1916588219. Advertising graffiti, not an address; nothing else in frame.
